title: Prompting, RAG or fine-tuning?
blurb: Choosing the right way to adapt a model to your problem.

slides.title: Three ways to adapt a model
body: When a model doesn’t do what you need out of the box, there are three main levers.
They solve different problems, and they differ a lot in cost and effort.

visual.caption: Roughly in order of effort, from least to most.

items.label: Prompting
items.text: Change the instructions and examples you send. Fast, cheap and easy to change.

items.label: Retrieval (RAG)
items.text: Find relevant documents and add them to the context when each question arrives.

items.label: Fine-tuning
items.text: Train the model further on your own examples, changing its parameters.

slides.title: Match the method to the problem
body: The key question is whether the model is missing knowledge or missing a behaviour.
Knowledge is usually best added through the context. Behaviour can often be shaped with prompts, and sometimes needs fine-tuning.

visual.caption: Common guidance — real projects often combine approaches.

items.heading: Missing knowledge → retrieval
items.text: Facts, documents and anything that changes over time.

items.heading: Missing behaviour → prompt first
items.text: A style, format or narrow task. Fine-tune if prompting can’t get there.

items.heading: Both → combine
items.text: For example, a fine-tuned model that answers from retrieved documents.

slides.title: Fine-tuning isn’t a knowledge upload
body: A common mistake is fine-tuning on documents to teach a model facts. It tends to work poorly: the model can still make things up, and the knowledge is hard to update or trace back to a source.
Fine-tuning is better at teaching how to respond than what to know. It also costs more: preparing data, training, testing, and repeating it when you change base models.

visual.caption: Illustrative comparison for a typical document Q&A project.
visual.question: We want a bot that answers questions about our staff handbook.

cards.label: Fine-tune on the handbook
cards.text: Hard to update, can’t show its sources, and may still make things up.

cards.label: Retrieve from the handbook
cards.text: Update the documents any time, and show which passage each answer used.

slides.title: Start simple, and measure
body: Each step up adds cost and complexity, so only take it when the simpler step has clearly fallen short.
Evaluation is what tells you whether it has.

visual.caption: A sensible default order for most projects.

items.heading: 1. Prompt well
items.text: Clear instructions and good examples solve more than you’d expect.

items.heading: 2. Add retrieval
items.text: When answers need knowledge the model doesn’t have.

items.heading: 3. Consider fine-tuning
items.text: When behaviour still falls short and you have plenty of good examples.

items.heading: Measure each step
items.text: Use an evaluation set to show each change actually helps.

quiz.question: An assistant must answer from policy documents that change every month. Which approach fits best?
quiz.explanation: Changing knowledge belongs in the context. Update the documents and the answers follow.

quiz.question: When is fine-tuning most likely to be worth it?
options: When you want the model to learn a set of facts
When the model needs to know about yesterday’s news
When you need a consistent behaviour or format that prompting can’t achieve, and have many good examples
Always — it’s the first thing to try
quiz.explanation: Fine-tuning shapes how a model responds. It’s worth the cost when prompting has clearly fallen short.

quiz.question: What’s usually the best first step?
quiz.explanation: Prompting is the cheapest and fastest lever, and often enough on its own.
